title: Creation, Annihilation, Fission and Fusion
topicTitle: Creation and annihilation; nuclear fission and fusion
notes: Annihilation occurs when a particle meets its antiparticle; rest mass may convert to photons while energy, momentum and charge remain conserved. For an electron and positron initially at rest, two photons travel in opposite directions so total momentum is zero.
An electron rest energy is mec²=0.511 MeV. An at-rest electron–positron pair can produce two 0.511 MeV photons, total energy 1.022 MeV.

Pair production is the reverse: a sufficiently energetic photon creates an electron and positron near a nucleus. The nucleus recoils, allowing momentum conservation; one photon cannot create the pair in empty space while conserving both energy and momentum.
The photon threshold is at least 2mec²=1.022 MeV. Any energy above threshold becomes kinetic energy of the pair and recoil.
Creation/annihilation of particle–antiparticle pairs is distinct from nuclear fission and fusion, although all processes obey mass-energy conservation.

Creation and annihilation convert rest mass into photons and photons into a pair, when energy and momentum can both be conserved. An electron and a positron at rest annihilate into at least two photons whose energies total 1.022 MeV. That is a different energy ledger from the 200 MeV of a fission.
confusion: A single photon cannot create a pair in free space while conserving momentum.
The 1.022 MeV threshold is specific to an electron–positron pair.

specificConditions: **Particle-Antiparticle Annihilation:** When a particle meets its antiparticle (e.g., $e^- + e^+$), they annihilate into pure energy (photons). Total mass-energy is conserved: $2m_e c^2 = 2 \times 0.511$ MeV = 1.022 MeV of gamma rays. Charge, lepton number, and momentum are also conserved.

**Pair Production (Creation):** The reverse of annihilation: a high-energy photon ($E > 1.022$ MeV) creates an $e^- e^+$ pair near a nucleus (to conserve momentum). The photon must have $E \ge 2m_e c^2$. Excess energy becomes kinetic energy of the pair.

**Fission vs Fusion in $BE/A$ Context:** Both processes release energy by moving toward the iron peak ($^{56}$Fe, $BE/A \approx 8.8$ MeV). Fission splits heavy nuclei ($A > 56$); fusion combines light nuclei ($A < 56$). Both increase the average binding energy per nucleon of the final products compared to initial reactants.
